implementation_notes: scala-xml is the standard XML library: build nodes with Elem/Text/NodeBuffer (or XML literals in Scala 2, which the compiler desugars into scala-xml calls; literals are dropped in Scala 3) and serialize with toString, while on the JVM javax.xml.transform applies XSLT stylesheets exactly as in Java. A transformer function returning NodeSeq or String is already the transformation, so the classic transformer object is unnecessary; it is justified only when several output formats share one interface.
pitfalls: XML literals are dropped in Scala 3: construct Elem/Text nodes explicitly (or use a library such as ScalaTags) and add scala-xml as an explicit dependency instead of relying on compiler desugaring.
scala-xml is community-maintained and decoupled from the compiler, so library/compiler version drift must be managed in the build.
NodeSeq operations are immutable and allocate: for very large documents prefer an iterator-based parser or streaming output over building the whole tree.

variants.name: JVM JAXP XSLT stylesheet
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative route on the JVM: TransformerFactory compiles the stylesheet and Transformer applies it from StreamSource to StreamResult, with per-request values passed through setParameter. Choose it when the presentation is a stylesheet maintained separately from the Scala code and the model can be serialized to XML.
variants.code_sketch:
import javax.xml.transform._
import javax.xml.transform.stream._

val tpl = TransformerFactory.newInstance()
  .newTemplates(new StreamSource("artist.xsl"))
tpl.newTransformer().transform(
  new StreamSource("artist.xml"), new StreamResult(System.out))
pitfalls: TransformerFactory/Transformer are not thread-safe: cache the Templates object, never a Transformer.
The JDK engine is XSLT 1.0; XSLT 2.0/3.0 features require Saxon on the classpath.
